title: Rank of an image batch tensor
prompt: An RGB image batch is stored in NCHW layout with shape $(8, 3, 24, 40)$. What is the rank of this tensor (its number of dimensions)?
hints: Rank is the length of the shape tuple, not the size of any single axis.
explanation:
The rank of a tensor is the number of axes, i.e. the length of its shape tuple. The shape $(8, 3, 24, 40)$ has four entries (batch N = 8, channels C = 3, height H = 24, width W = 40), so the rank is 4.

Typical wrong answers: 8 is the batch size (the size of the first axis, not the number of axes); 3 is the number of colour channels; 5 would need an additional axis, such as time or depth in a video or volumetric batch.

title: Which setting is supervised classification?
prompt: Which example is supervised image classification?

options.text: Learn actions from rewards in an environment.
options.explanation: This describes reinforcement learning: the agent receives a scalar reward for its actions, not a correct label for every input.

options.text: Train on labeled images to predict the class of new images.
options.explanation: Supervised learning uses input-label pairs during training, and classification means the label is a discrete class predicted for unseen images.

options.text: Predict masked patches using targets from the same image.
options.explanation: This is self-supervised learning (as in masked autoencoders): the targets are generated from the data itself rather than provided by human-assigned class labels.

options.text: Cluster unlabeled images by appearance.
options.explanation: Clustering is unsupervised learning: no labels are used, and the groups found are not predefined classes.

explanation: The learning paradigm is decided by where the training signal comes from. Supervised learning has explicit labels for each training example, reinforcement learning has rewards, self-supervised learning builds targets from the input itself, and unsupervised learning has no targets at all. Supervised image classification is the case with labeled images and a class prediction for new ones.

title: What makes image classification harder?
prompt: Which changes can make image classification harder? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The lighting changes from daylight to dim indoor lighting.
options.explanation: Illumination changes alter pixel intensities and colours drastically even though the object is the same, so the model must be robust to them.

options.text: Class names are renamed consistently throughout the dataset.
options.explanation: A class name is only a label string; renaming it consistently changes neither the images nor how separable the classes are, so the difficulty stays the same.

options.text: The object is partly hidden behind another object.
options.explanation: Occlusion removes part of the evidence, so the model has to recognise the class from incomplete visual information.

options.text: The object is photographed from a different viewpoint.
options.explanation: Viewpoint changes the object's appearance in pixel space a lot (different visible parts, shape and scale), so the same class looks very different.

explanation: Classification is hard because the same class can look very different in pixel space: lighting, viewpoint, occlusion, scale, background clutter and deformation all change the pixels without changing the label. Changes to the pixels matter; consistently renaming the labels does not, because it is a pure relabeling of the output.

title: Reducing a generalization gap
prompt: A model fits the training data well but generalizes poorly. Which changes can reduce overfitting? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Choose model complexity using validation results.
options.explanation: Validation performance shows when added capacity starts to hurt generalization, so selecting complexity on it avoids a model that is too flexible.

options.text: Add representative labeled training examples.
options.explanation: More data that covers the real distribution constrains the model, so it can no longer memorize idiosyncrasies of a small training set.

options.text: Add suitable regularization that penalizes large weights.
options.explanation: A penalty such as L2 weight decay discourages large weights and therefore overly wiggly functions, reducing the effective model complexity.

options.text: Repeatedly tune hyperparameters on the final test set.
options.explanation: Tuning on the test set leaks test information into the model choice, so the test score becomes optimistic and no longer measures generalization. Tuning belongs on a validation set.

explanation: Overfitting means the model has adapted to the training set instead of the underlying distribution. The remedies are to limit complexity (regularization, model selection on validation data) and to provide more representative data. The test set must stay untouched until the end; using it for tuning only hides overfitting, it does not reduce it.

title: Two layers without a nonlinearity
prompt: Two layers compute $h = W_1 x + b_1$ and $y = W_2 h + b_2$, with no nonlinearity between them. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The output must be zero for every input.
options.explanation: Nothing forces the output to vanish: $y = W_2W_1x + W_2b_1 + b_2$ is generally non-zero. Only the weights and biases decide its value.

options.text: The result is necessarily nonlinear.
options.explanation: A composition of affine maps is affine, never nonlinear in the sense of being more expressive. Stacking linear layers alone does not add nonlinearity.

options.text: The result is one affine map with weight $W_2W_1$ and bias $W_2b_1+b_2$.
options.explanation: Substituting gives $y = W_2(W_1x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2b_1 + b_2)$, a single affine map.

options.text: Backpropagation is impossible without an activation.
options.explanation: The chain rule works through affine layers just fine (gradients are products with $W_2^\top$ and $W_1^\top$). Activations are needed for expressiveness, not for backprop to be possible.

explanation:
Substituting $h$ into $y$ gives

$$y = W_2(W_1x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2b_1 + b_2),$$

so the two layers collapse into one affine layer. This is why deep networks need a nonlinearity between layers: without it, depth adds no representational power.

title: Interpreting a large accuracy gap
prompt: A classifier has 99% training accuracy and 69% validation accuracy on comparable datasets. What does this gap suggest?

options.text: Validation accuracy must exceed training accuracy.
options.explanation: Here it is the reverse: training accuracy is 30 points higher. Nothing requires validation accuracy to be higher, and normally it is equal or lower because the model has not seen those examples.

options.text: The gap suggests overfitting.
options.explanation: Near-perfect training accuracy with much lower accuracy on held-out data means the model memorized training specifics that do not generalize.

options.text: Every validation label must be wrong.
options.explanation: If all labels were wrong, accuracy would be near 0 (or chance-level for noise), not 69%. A gap of this kind does not imply label errors.

options.text: The model must underfit both datasets.
options.explanation: Underfitting means poor performance on the training data too. 99% training accuracy shows the model fits the training set very well.

explanation: Compare training and validation performance: both low means underfitting, both high means a good fit, and high training with clearly lower validation performance (a large generalization gap) means overfitting. The datasets being comparable rules out distribution shift as the obvious explanation.

title: Output of a semantic segmentation model
prompt: A semantic segmentation model uses 5 classes, labeled 0 to 4. What is the final label output for a $20 \times 30$ image?

options.text: A list of object bounding boxes.
options.explanation: Bounding boxes are the output of object detection. Semantic segmentation labels pixels, not boxes.

options.text: One class label for the whole image.
options.explanation: A single label per image is image classification. Segmentation must say which class each pixel belongs to.

options.text: A $20 \times 30$ array whose entries are integers from 0 to 4.
options.explanation: Segmentation assigns one class index to every pixel, so the label map has the image's spatial size, with entries in $\{0, \dots, 4\}$.

options.text: A single scalar confidence score.
options.explanation: One scalar cannot describe a per-pixel labeling. Confidence scores may exist internally, but they are not the label output.

explanation: Semantic segmentation is dense prediction: every pixel gets a class. Internally the network usually produces a score map of shape $(5, 20, 30)$, one channel per class, and taking the argmax over the class axis gives the final $20 \times 30$ integer label map.

title: Softmax of a small score vector
prompt: What is $\operatorname{softmax}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\right)$? Round each probability to two decimal places.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0.00 & 1.00 & 0.00\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This is a hard argmax (one-hot) vector. Softmax is smooth: a score gap of 2 gives the other classes $e^0/9.39 \approx 0.11$, not exactly 0.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0.25 & 0.50 & 0.25\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This would be the result of a score gap of $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$ (since $e^{0.69} \approx 2$). With a gap of 2 the largest entry is $e^2 \approx 7.39$ times bigger than the others, not 2 times.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0.79 & 0.11 & 0.11\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The 0.79 sits on the wrong position. Softmax is monotonic, so the largest probability belongs to the largest score, which is the middle entry.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0.11 & 0.79 & 0.11\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: $e^0 = 1$, $e^2 \approx 7.389$, sum $\approx 9.389$, so the probabilities are $1/9.389 \approx 0.11$, $7.389/9.389 \approx 0.79$ and $0.11$.

explanation: Softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the sum: $p_i = e^{s_i} / \sum_j e^{s_j}$. Here the exponentials are $(1, 7.389, 1)$ with sum $9.389$, giving $(0.107, 0.787, 0.107) \approx (0.11, 0.79, 0.11)$. The largest score gets the largest probability, but the others keep a non-zero share.

title: Multiclass hinge loss
prompt:
A classifier gives scores $s_{\text{dog}} = 4$, $s_{\text{cat}} = 2$ and $s_{\text{ship}} = 1$. The true class is cat. With margin 1, compute the multiclass hinge loss

$$L = \sum_{j \neq \text{cat}} \max\left(0,\, s_j - s_{\text{cat}} + 1\right).$$
hints: Only the two wrong classes contribute a term each.
A term is zero when the wrong class's score is at least the margin below the true score.
explanation:
dog: $\max(0, 4 - 2 + 1) = 3$, because dog scores above the true class. ship: $\max(0, 1 - 2 + 1) = \max(0, 0) = 0$, because ship is exactly one margin below cat, which is allowed. The true class is excluded from the sum, so $L = 3 + 0 = 3$.

Typical wrong results: 5 comes from adding the wrong-class scores $4 + 1$ instead of the margin violations; 0 comes from forgetting that dog beats the true class; 2 comes from dropping the margin (+1) in the dog term, $4 - 2 = 2$.

title: Broadcasting a bias-like vector
prompt: Adding tensors of shapes $(6, 4)$ and $(4,)$ uses standard NumPy/PyTorch broadcasting. What is the output shape?

options.text: It raises a shape error.
options.explanation: Broadcasting compares shapes from the trailing axis: the last axes are both 4, and the missing leading axis of the second tensor is treated as size 1, so the shapes are compatible.
Element-wise addition never reduces an axis. The result has at least as many dimensions as the larger input.
The vector $(4,)$ is viewed as $(1, 4)$ and repeated across the 6 rows, so the result has shape $(6, 4)$.
Broadcasting keeps the axis order of the inputs; it does not transpose. The 4-axis stays the last one.

explanation: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, pads the shorter shape with leading 1s and stretches size-1 axes. Here $(4,) \to (1, 4) \to (6, 4)$. This is exactly how a bias vector is added to every row of a batch of activations.

title: One filter application on a 2x2 patch
prompt:
Apply the filter

$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$$

to the patch

$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5\\1 & 6\end{bmatrix}$$

using cross-correlation (no kernel flipping) and no bias. What is the output?
hints: Multiply entries at the same position and add everything up.
explanation:
Cross-correlation multiplies the filter and patch element-wise at matching positions and sums: $1\cdot 2 + 0\cdot 5 + 0\cdot 1 + (-1)\cdot 6 = 2 - 6 = -4$.

Typical wrong results: 4 is the answer of a true convolution, where the kernel is flipped first (flipped kernel $[[-1, 0], [0, 1]]$ gives $-2 + 6 = 4$); 8 comes from adding $2 + 6$ and ignoring the minus sign of the filter; -1 comes from pairing the filter entries with the wrong patch positions, e.g. $1\cdot 1 + (-1)\cdot 2$.

title: Spatial output size of a strided convolution
prompt: A convolution has a $10 \times 13$ input, a $3 \times 3$ kernel, stride 2, padding 1 per side and dilation 1. Using floor rounding, what is the spatial output size?

options.text: $6 \times 7$
options.explanation: The height formula gives $\lfloor 9/2 \rfloor + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5$; rounding 4.5 up to 5 before adding 1 would give 6, but the output size uses floor.

options.text: $5 \times 7$
options.explanation: Height: $\lfloor (10 + 2 - 3)/2 \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor 4.5 \rfloor + 1 = 5$. Width: $\lfloor (13 + 2 - 3)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7$.

options.text: $10 \times 13$
options.explanation: The size would be preserved only for stride 1 with 'same'-style padding. A stride of 2 roughly halves each spatial dimension.

options.text: $5 \times 6$
options.explanation: The width is wrong: $(13 + 2 - 3)/2 = 6$ counts the strides between positions, and the first window position adds the missing $+1$, giving 7.

explanation: For each spatial dimension $$O = \left\lfloor \frac{n + 2p - d(k-1) - 1}{s} \right\rfloor + 1,$$ which with $d = 1$ becomes $\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$. Height: $\lfloor 9/2 \rfloor + 1 = 5$. Width: $\lfloor 12/2 \rfloor + 1 = 7$. Always compute each dimension separately and floor the division before adding 1.

title: Parameters of a standard convolution
prompt: A convolution with groups=1 maps 4 input channels to 10 output channels using $3 \times 3$ kernels and one bias per output channel. How many trainable parameters does it have?
hints: Each output channel has one filter spanning all input channels.
Add the biases at the end.
explanation:
Weights: $C_{out} \cdot C_{in} \cdot k_h \cdot k_w = 10 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 360$. Biases: one per output channel, 10. Total $360 + 10 = 370$.

Typical wrong results: 360 forgets the bias; 46 is a single filter-sized count, $4\cdot 9 + 10$ (one filter's weights plus all biases); 400 is $10 \cdot 4 \cdot 10$, i.e. counting 10 values per input-output channel pair (a bias attached to every filter slice) instead of 9 weights, with the biases added once at the end.

title: Effect of increasing dilation
prompt: A $3 \times 3$ convolution keeps its channel counts fixed. Dilation increases from 1 to 3. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The number of learned kernel weights stays the same.
options.explanation: Dilation only spaces the taps of the kernel apart; there are still $3 \times 3 = 9$ weights per input-output channel pair.

options.text: Each input-output channel pair must gain 49 learned weights.
options.explanation: 49 is the size of the $7 \times 7$ footprint, but the positions in between are skipped (not learned zeros). Each pair still has only 9 weights.

options.text: The output channel count necessarily triples.
options.explanation: The number of output channels is chosen by the layer definition ($C_{out}$), and the problem says the channel counts are kept fixed. Dilation does not change it.

options.text: The effective spatial footprint increases from $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$.
options.explanation: The effective kernel size is $d(k-1) + 1 = 3 \cdot 2 + 1 = 7$, so the same 9 weights cover a $7 \times 7$ area.

explanation: Dilation inserts gaps of $d-1$ positions between kernel taps. The effective size becomes $d(k-1) + 1$, which grows from 3 to 7 for $k = 3$ and $d = 3$, while the parameter count $C_{out}C_{in}k^2$ is unchanged. This makes dilation a cheap way to enlarge the receptive field.

title: Valid numbers of groups
prompt: A grouped convolution has 16 input channels and 24 output channels. Which numbers of groups are valid? (Select all that apply.)

options.explanation: 2 divides both 16 and 24, giving groups of 8 input and 12 output channels.
6 divides 24, but 16 / 6 is not an integer, so the input channels cannot be split evenly. The group count must divide both channel numbers.
8 divides both 16 and 24 (it is their greatest common divisor), giving groups of 2 input and 3 output channels.
4 divides both 16 and 24, giving groups of 4 input and 6 output channels.

explanation: In a grouped convolution the input channels and the output channels are each split into $g$ equal groups, so $g$ must divide both $C_{in}$ and $C_{out}$. The valid values are the common divisors of 16 and 24, i.e. the divisors of $\gcd(16, 24) = 8$: 1, 2, 4 and 8. Dividing only one of the two numbers (as 6 does for 24) is not enough.

title: Weights of a depthwise convolution
prompt: A depthwise convolution has 6 input channels, 12 output channels, groups=6 and a $3 \times 3$ kernel. With no bias, how many weights does it have?
hints: With groups, each output channel only sees $C_{in}/\text{groups}$ input channels.
How many output channels are there in total?
explanation:
Weight count $= C_{out} \cdot (C_{in}/\text{groups}) \cdot k_h \cdot k_w = 12 \cdot (6/6) \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 12 \cdot 1 \cdot 9 = 108$. Each of the 6 groups has one input channel and 2 output channels, so there are 12 single-channel $3\times 3$ filters.

Typical wrong results: 120 adds 12 biases although there is no bias; 648 ignores the grouping ($12 \cdot 6 \cdot 9$, the groups=1 count); 54 counts only 6 filters ($6 \cdot 9$) and forgets that each input channel feeds 2 output channels.

title: Properties of a 1x1 convolution
prompt: A $1 \times 1$ convolution maps 6 channels to 9, with stride 1, groups=1, no padding and no bias. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can mix input channels at each spatial location.
options.explanation: Each output channel is a weighted sum over all 6 input channels at the same pixel, i.e. a per-pixel linear map $\mathbb{R}^6 \to \mathbb{R}^9$.

options.text: It preserves height and width.
options.explanation: With kernel 1, stride 1 and no padding, $O = \lfloor (n - 1)/1 \rfloor + 1 = n$, so the spatial size is unchanged.

options.text: It directly mixes neighboring spatial locations.
options.explanation: A $1 \times 1$ kernel only looks at a single pixel position, so there is no spatial mixing; that requires a larger kernel (or a pooling or other spatial layer).

options.text: It uses 54 learned weights.
options.explanation: $C_{out} \cdot C_{in} \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 9 \cdot 6 = 54$, and there is no bias.

explanation: A $1 \times 1$ convolution applies the same fully connected layer independently at every pixel. It changes the channel count and mixes channels, keeps the spatial size with stride 1 and no padding, and has $C_{out}C_{in}$ weights (here 54). It cannot combine information from neighbouring pixels.

title: Receptive field of stacked convolutions
prompt: Four consecutive convolutions have $3 \times 3$ kernels, stride 1, dilation 1 and no padding. The receptive field of one final output value is a square. What is its side length in input pixels?
hints: Each additional stride-1 layer extends the receptive field by $k-1$.
Start from a receptive field of 1 for a single output value.
explanation:
With stride 1 each layer adds $k - 1 = 2$ pixels: $r = 1 + 4 \cdot 2 = 9$. Equivalently the receptive field grows $1 \to 3 \to 5 \to 7 \to 9$, so the final output depends on a $9 \times 9$ input region.

Typical wrong results: 7 is the value after only three layers; 8 forgets the initial $+1$ ($4 \cdot 2$); 12 multiplies the kernel sizes ($4 \cdot 3$) as if each layer added a full kernel, ignoring the overlap between neighbouring windows.

title: Max pooling on a 4x4 input
prompt:
Apply $2 \times 2$ max pooling with stride 2 and no padding to this single-channel input, starting at the top-left:

$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 & 7\\4 & 3 & 5 & 2\\6 & -1 & 3 & 4\\0 & 2 & 8 & 1\end{bmatrix}$$

What is the output matrix?

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}7 & 4\\8 & 6\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: These are the right maxima, but the windows are read in the wrong order (the columns are mirrored). The top-left window's maximum is 4 and goes into the top-left output position.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}4 & 7\\6 & 8\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The four non-overlapping windows have maxima $\max(2,1,4,3) = 4$, $\max(0,7,5,2) = 7$, $\max(6,-1,0,2) = 6$ and $\max(3,4,8,1) = 8$.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\6 & 3\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: These are the top-left entries of each window, i.e. plain subsampling with stride 2. Max pooling takes the maximum of each window, not its first element.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}4 & 5\\2 & 8\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The entries 5 and 2 are not window maxima: the top-right window $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7\\5 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has maximum 7 and the bottom-left window $\begin{bmatrix}6 & -1\\0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has maximum 6. The windows must be non-overlapping blocks.

explanation: With a $2 \times 2$ window and stride 2 the $4 \times 4$ input splits into four non-overlapping $2 \times 2$ blocks, and each block is replaced by its maximum, giving a $2 \times 2$ output $\begin{bmatrix}4 & 7\\6 & 8\end{bmatrix}$. The output size is $\lfloor (4 - 2)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 2$ in each dimension.

title: Gradient through a max-pooling window
prompt: A max-pooling window is $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 7\\4 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. The loss gradient at its output is $-3$. No other operation contributes gradients. What is the input gradient?

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The position is right but the sign is flipped. Max pooling is locally the identity on the winning element, so the upstream gradient $-3$ is passed unchanged.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}-3 & -3\\-3 & -3\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: Copying the gradient to every position is not what max pooling does; only the element that produced the output affects it, so the others get zero gradient.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}-0.75 & -0.75\\-0.75 & -0.75\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: Splitting the gradient equally ($-3/4$ each) is the backward pass of average pooling, not max pooling.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3\\0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The maximum 7 is at the top-right position, so it receives the full upstream gradient $-3$, and all other positions receive 0.

explanation: Max pooling outputs $\max_i x_i$, whose derivative is 1 for the argmax element and 0 for all others. Backpropagation therefore routes the upstream gradient entirely to the position of the maximum (here 7, top-right) and sends zero elsewhere. Average pooling, in contrast, would distribute the gradient evenly.

title: Why a nonlinearity is needed between layers
prompt: Explain why stacking two linear (affine) layers without an activation function in between gives no more expressive power than a single layer, and what an activation function changes.
model_answer: Two affine layers compute $y = W_2(W_1x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2W_1)x + (W_2b_1 + b_2)$, which is again a single affine map, so extra depth adds nothing and the model can only represent linear decision boundaries. A nonlinearity such as ReLU between the layers prevents this algebraic collapse, so the composition can represent nonlinear functions and deeper networks become more expressive. Backpropagation itself works either way; the nonlinearity is needed for expressiveness, not for gradients to exist.
key_points: Composition of affine maps is affine: $W_2W_1$ and bias $W_2b_1 + b_2$.
Depth without a nonlinearity adds no representational power (only linear or affine functions).
A nonlinearity between layers breaks the collapse and enables nonlinear functions.
Backprop still works without activations; the issue is expressiveness.
hints: Substitute the first layer's output into the second.
Can a single affine map separate classes that are not linearly separable?
explanation: The key step is the substitution that merges the two weight matrices into one product matrix and the two biases into one bias. A good answer also states the consequence (only linear/affine functions, so no depth benefit) and what fixes it (an elementwise nonlinearity between layers). A common half-answer says only that 'activations add nonlinearity' without showing why the layers collapse; another common mistake is claiming backpropagation would be impossible without activations, which is false.

title: Comparing standard, depthwise, grouped and 1x1 convolutions
prompt: Compare a standard convolution, a grouped/depthwise convolution and a $1 \times 1$ convolution in terms of what they mix (channels versus spatial positions) and how their weight counts scale. Why can combining a depthwise and a $1 \times 1$ convolution be attractive?
model_answer: A standard $k \times k$ convolution mixes all input channels and neighbouring pixels at once and has $C_{out}C_{in}k^2$ weights. A grouped convolution with $g$ groups only mixes channels inside each group, so it has $C_{out}(C_{in}/g)k^2$ weights; the depthwise case ($g = C_{in}$) mixes no channels and only filters spatially. A $1 \times 1$ convolution does the opposite: it mixes channels at each pixel with $C_{out}C_{in}$ weights but no spatial neighbours. A depthwise convolution followed by a $1 \times 1$ convolution therefore splits spatial and channel mixing into two cheap steps and needs far fewer parameters than one standard convolution.
key_points: Standard convolution mixes channels and space together with $C_{out}C_{in}k^2$ weights.
Grouped convolution reduces weights by a factor $g$ and mixes channels only within groups; depthwise means no channel mixing.
A $1 \times 1$ convolution mixes channels per pixel with $C_{out}C_{in}$ weights and no spatial mixing.
Depthwise plus $1 \times 1$ separates spatial and channel mixing, giving a large parameter saving.
hints: Write the weight count formula for each of the three layer types.
Which of the layers can see neighbouring pixels, and which can see other channels?
explanation: Keep the two kinds of mixing apart: spatial mixing needs a kernel larger than 1, channel mixing needs connections across channels. Standard convolution does both with the largest weight count; depthwise does only spatial and $1 \times 1$ does only channel mixing, so their combination approximates a standard convolution at a fraction of the cost. For example, 6 to 12 channels with $3\times 3$ kernels needs 648 weights standard, 108 depthwise-style (groups=6) and 72 for a $1\times 1$ map. Half-answers usually quote only the formulas and forget what each layer can or cannot mix.

title: Sigmoid derivative for a large preactivation
prompt: A sigmoid unit has preactivation 15. What happens to its local derivative?

options.text: Saturation forces its output to be zero-centered.
options.explanation: The sigmoid output always lies in (0, 1), so it is never zero-centered. At preactivation 15 the output is essentially 1, which is the saturated end of the range, not a centred value.

options.text: Its derivative is exactly 15.
options.explanation: The derivative is $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$, which never exceeds 0.25. The number 15 is the preactivation (the input of the sigmoid), not its slope.

options.text: Its derivative is very small because the unit is saturated.
options.explanation: At $x=15$, $\sigma(15)\approx 1-3\times10^{-7}$, so $\sigma'(15)=\sigma(15)(1-\sigma(15))\approx 3\times 10^{-7}$. The curve is almost flat there, so very little gradient flows back.

options.text: Its derivative grows without bound as the preactivation increases.
options.explanation: The derivative peaks at 0.25 for $x=0$ and decays towards 0 on both sides as $|x|$ grows. Only the preactivation itself grows without bound.

hints: Recall the formula for the derivative of the sigmoid in terms of its output.
What is the sigmoid output when the input is 15?
explanation: The sigmoid derivative is $\sigma'(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$, which is at most 0.25 and tends to 0 for large positive or negative $x$. For preactivation 15 the output is almost exactly 1, so the factor $1-\sigma(x)$ is about $3\times10^{-7}$ and the local derivative is tiny. This is the saturation (vanishing gradient) problem: a saturated unit passes almost no gradient to the layers before it.

title: Properties of tanh
prompt: For finite real inputs in exact arithmetic, which statements about tanh are correct?

options.text: tanh(0) = 0.
options.explanation: $\tanh(x)=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}$ and at $x=0$ the numerator is $1-1=0$. This is why tanh is zero-centered.

options.text: Its output lies strictly between -1 and 1.
options.explanation: Since $e^{-x}>0$ for every finite $x$, the numerator magnitude is strictly smaller than the denominator, so $|\tanh(x)|<1$. The values $\pm 1$ are only approached as limits.

options.text: Its derivative approaches 1 as the input magnitude grows.
options.explanation: The derivative is $1-\tanh^2(x)$. It equals 1 only at $x=0$ and tends to 0 for large $|x|$. It is the output (not the derivative) that approaches $\pm1$, which is what makes this tempting.

options.text: Changing the input sign changes the output sign.
options.explanation: tanh is an odd function: $\tanh(-x)=-\tanh(x)$. Flipping the input sign therefore flips the output sign (and leaves 0 at 0).

hints: Write tanh in terms of exponentials and check its value at 0 and its symmetry.
The derivative of tanh is $1-\tanh^2(x)$.
explanation: tanh is an odd, zero-centered, bounded function whose outputs stay strictly inside (-1, 1) for finite inputs. Its derivative $1-\tanh^2(x)$ is largest (equal to 1) at the origin and vanishes in the saturated tails, so tanh also suffers from vanishing gradients. Do not confuse the limit of the output ($\pm1$) with the limit of the derivative (0).

title: Evaluating a Leaky ReLU
prompt: Leaky ReLU is defined by $f(x)=x$ for $x\ge 0$ and $f(x)=0.05x$ for $x<0$. Compute $f(-4)$. Give the answer with 2 decimals.
hints: Decide which branch of the definition applies to a negative input.
Multiply the input by the negative-side slope.
explanation: Since $-4<0$, the second branch applies: $f(-4)=0.05\cdot(-4)=-0.20$. Typical wrong results: 0 is the output of a plain ReLU (which ignores the small negative slope); 0.20 loses the sign; -4 uses the identity branch as if the input were non-negative (slope 1 instead of 0.05).

title: PReLU versus Leaky ReLU
prompt: Which statements about standard PReLU and Leaky ReLU are correct?

options.text: PReLU learns its negative-side slope during training.
options.explanation: PReLU computes $f(x)=x$ for $x\ge0$ and $f(x)=ax$ for $x<0$, where $a$ is a trainable parameter updated by backpropagation like any weight.

options.text: Leaky ReLU uses a fixed negative-side slope hyperparameter.
options.explanation: Leaky ReLU uses a constant slope (e.g. 0.01 or 0.05) chosen by the designer and not updated during training.

options.text: PReLU has no trainable slope parameter.
options.explanation: The 'P' stands for parametric: the negative slope is exactly the trainable parameter that distinguishes PReLU from Leaky ReLU.

options.text: Both necessarily output zero for every negative input.
options.explanation: That describes plain ReLU. Leaky ReLU and PReLU output slope times input, which is non-zero for negative inputs whenever the slope is non-zero; this keeps a gradient flowing and avoids dead units.

hints: What does the first letter of PReLU stand for?
What problem were the negative-side slopes introduced to solve?
explanation: Both activations replace the flat zero of ReLU on the negative side by a linear piece with a small slope, so negative inputs still pass some gradient. They differ only in how the slope is obtained: Leaky ReLU fixes it as a hyperparameter, PReLU learns it (per channel or shared) as a parameter. Neither is identically zero for negative inputs.

title: Elementwise output of ReLU6
prompt: ReLU6 is $f(x)=\min(\max(0,x),6)$. What is its elementwise output for $\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & 9\end{bmatrix}$?

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This applies only the upper cap at 6 and forgets the lower clipping: $\max(0,-2)=0$, not -2.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}$
$\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 9\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This is the plain ReLU result. ReLU6 additionally caps the output at 6, so 9 becomes 6.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 6 & 6\end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The value 4 is already below the cap, so $\min(4,6)=4$. Only entries above 6 are changed by the cap.

hints: Apply max(0, x) first, then min(., 6), entry by entry.
Entries between 0 and 6 pass through unchanged.
explanation: ReLU6 is a ReLU whose output is clipped to the interval [0, 6]: negatives become 0, values in [0, 6] stay as they are, and values above 6 become 6. Applying this elementwise to -2, 4, 9 gives 0, 4, 6.

title: Maxout with three affine candidates
prompt: A Maxout unit has three separate affine candidates with values -2, 5 and 1. Which statements are correct?

options.text: It outputs the average 4/3.
options.explanation: The arithmetic $(-2+5+1)/3=4/3$ is right, but Maxout does not average its candidates; it takes their maximum.

options.text: It is identical to spatial max pooling on the input image.
options.explanation: Maxout takes a max over several learned affine functions of the same input. Max pooling takes a max over fixed spatial positions of a window and has no learned weights, so the two are different operations.

options.text: Its output is 5.
options.explanation: Maxout outputs $\max_k (w_k^\top x + b_k)$, and the largest of -2, 5 and 1 is 5.

options.text: Three affine candidates with the same input width use three times the weights of one candidate.
options.explanation: Each candidate has its own weight vector of the same length as the input, so three candidates need three times as many weights (and biases) as one.

hints: Which operation combines the candidates: sum, mean or max?
Does each candidate share its weights with the others?
explanation: A Maxout unit computes several affine functions of the same input and outputs the largest one, here max(-2, 5, 1) = 5. Because every candidate has its own weights, the parameter count grows linearly with the number of candidates. Maxout is therefore a learned piecewise-linear activation, not an average and not a fixed spatial pooling.

title: BatchNorm statistics in evaluation mode
prompt: BatchNorm tracks running statistics during training. Which statistics does it use in evaluation mode?

options.text: The labels in the test batch.
options.explanation: Normalization layers never use labels; using test labels would also be leakage. BatchNorm only uses feature statistics.

options.text: The previous optimizer step's gradients.
options.explanation: Gradients are used to update parameters, not to normalize activations. BatchNorm's statistics are means and variances of activations.

options.text: Only the current test sample's mean and variance.
options.explanation: That would be per-sample normalization (like instance/layer normalization) and would make outputs unstable, especially for a batch of one. BatchNorm in eval mode ignores the current batch's statistics.

options.text: Running mean and variance accumulated during training.
options.explanation: During training BatchNorm updates an exponential moving average of the batch means and variances; in eval mode these fixed values are used so the output for a sample does not depend on the other samples in the batch.

hints: Eval mode should be deterministic and independent of the other test samples.
What did the layer store while it was training?
explanation: In training mode BatchNorm normalizes with the mean and variance of the current mini-batch and updates running estimates of them. In evaluation mode it switches to those stored running estimates, so predictions are deterministic and do not depend on batch composition or batch size. Forgetting to call model.eval() is a classic cause of poor or inconsistent test results.

title: Convolution bias followed by BatchNorm
prompt: A convolution is followed immediately by BatchNorm with a learned scale and shift. Why is a separate convolutional bias often unnecessary?

options.text: BatchNorm requires the convolution to double spatial resolution.
options.explanation: BatchNorm is applied per channel and does not change or constrain the spatial size of the convolution output.

options.text: BatchNorm makes the convolutional weights non-trainable.
options.explanation: The convolution weights still receive gradients through BatchNorm and are trained as usual. BatchNorm only rescales and shifts the activations.

options.text: A convolution with bias cannot be differentiated.
options.explanation: A bias is just an added constant per channel and is trivially differentiable (its gradient is the sum of the upstream gradient). The bias is redundant, not undifferentiable.

options.text: Subtracting the channel mean cancels a constant bias, and BatchNorm learns its own shift.
options.explanation: A per-channel constant $b$ shifts the channel mean by $b$ and leaves the variance unchanged, so $(x+b)-\mu_{x+b}=x-\mu_x$. BatchNorm's learnable shift $\beta$ then provides the offset the network actually needs.

hints: What happens to the batch mean of a channel when a constant is added to every value?
Which BatchNorm parameter already plays the role of a per-channel offset?
explanation: BatchNorm first subtracts the per-channel batch mean, so any constant per-channel offset added by the convolution is removed before it can influence the output. The layer then adds its own learnable shift $\beta$, which does the job of the bias. Dropping the convolution bias (bias=False) saves parameters without losing expressiveness.

title: Normalization with tiny per-device batches
prompt: Training uses 2 images per device, and BatchNorm statistics are unreliable. Why can GroupNorm help?

options.text: GroupNorm automatically increases the physical batch size.
options.explanation: GroupNorm does not change how many images are processed together. It simply does not need a large batch because its statistics do not come from the batch dimension.

options.text: GroupNorm removes all learned convolution weights.
options.explanation: The convolution weights stay in the network and remain trainable. GroupNorm only adds an optional learned per-channel scale and shift.

options.text: GroupNorm computes statistics within each sample rather than aggregating across the batch.
options.explanation: For each sample, GroupNorm splits the channels into groups and normalizes over the channels in a group and the spatial positions. The result is independent of the batch size and of the other samples.

options.text: GroupNorm estimates its running mean from the final test set.
options.explanation: GroupNorm keeps no running statistics at all; it computes them on the fly for every sample, in training and testing alike. Using test-set statistics would also be leakage.

hints: Which axes does BatchNorm average over, and what happens when the batch axis has size 2?
Does GroupNorm need a different behaviour in training and evaluation?
explanation: BatchNorm estimates mean and variance across the batch, so with 2 images per device those estimates are very noisy. GroupNorm computes them per sample over groups of channels and spatial positions, so its behaviour does not depend on the batch size and is identical at training and test time. That is why it is the usual choice for detection, segmentation and other small-batch settings.

title: Concatenating NCHW feature maps
prompt: Two NCHW feature maps have shapes $(4,6,12,12)$ and $(4,10,12,12)$. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Concatenating them along the channel axis produces $(4,16,12,12)$.
options.explanation: Concatenation adds the sizes along the chosen axis: $6+10=16$ channels, while batch (4) and spatial size (12×12) are unchanged.

options.text: Channel concatenation computes the elementwise sum of their feature values.
options.explanation: Concatenation stacks the channels side by side and keeps every value separately. Summing is a different operation (elementwise addition, as in residual connections).

options.text: Elementwise addition without broadcasting is valid for these shapes.
options.explanation: Addition needs equal shapes, but the channel dimensions differ (6 versus 10). Broadcasting cannot rescue this because neither of them is 1.

options.text: Channel concatenation requires matching batch and spatial dimensions.
options.explanation: All dimensions except the concatenation axis must agree, so batch size, height and width must match; only the channel count may differ.

hints: Which axis may differ when concatenating, and which must match?
Can a tensor with 6 channels be broadcast against one with 10?
explanation: Concatenation along an axis sums that axis and requires all other axes to be equal, giving $(4,16,12,12)$ here. Elementwise addition instead requires identical (or broadcastable) shapes and mixes the values into one tensor of the same shape. U-Net style skip connections use concatenation, ResNet-style shortcuts use addition.

title: Shape after a U-Net skip concatenation
prompt: A U-Net upsampling layer produces a $32 \times 20 \times 20$ feature map ($C \times H \times W$). A skip feature has the same shape. What is their shape after concatenation along channels?

options.text: $64 \times 10 \times 10$
options.explanation: The channel count is right, but concatenation along channels leaves the spatial size untouched; nothing here halves it to 10×10.

options.text: $96 \times 10 \times 10$
options.explanation: Both inputs have 32 channels, so there is no way to get 96, and the spatial size also stays 20×20.

options.text: $64 \times 20 \times 20$
options.explanation: Channels add up to $32+32=64$, while height and width stay at 20×20.

options.text: $32 \times 20 \times 20$
options.explanation: This would be the result of elementwise addition (or of ignoring the skip feature). Concatenation stacks the channels, doubling them.

hints: Which dimension grows under channel concatenation?
Do height and width change?
explanation: Concatenating along the channel axis adds the channel counts and keeps the spatial dimensions, so $32+32=64$ channels at 20×20. This doubling is why the convolution after a U-Net skip connection usually takes twice as many input channels as the upsampled feature has.

title: U-Net bottleneck size
prompt: A U-Net has encoder widths $(16,32,64,128)$, i.e. four encoder stages. Each stage after the first starts with $2 \times 2$ max pooling at stride 2. All convolutions preserve spatial size. For a $160 \times 160$ input, what is the side length of the bottleneck feature map (in pixels)?
hints: Count how many stages start with pooling; the first stage does not.
Each pooling halves the side length.
explanation: There are 4 stages and the first one has no pooling, so pooling is applied 3 times: $160\to80\to40\to20$. The bottleneck side is $160/2^3=20$. Typical wrong results: 80 (counting only one pooling), 40 (two poolings) and 10 (pooling in all four stages, including the first).

title: Properties of transposed convolution
prompt: Which statements about a bias-free transposed convolution are correct?

options.text: It can increase spatial resolution when an appropriate stride is used.
options.explanation: With stride $s>1$ the output size is roughly $s$ times the input size, e.g. $H_{out}=(H-1)s-2p+d(k-1)+p_{out}+1$. This is why it is used for learned upsampling.

options.text: It always computes the exact inverse of the corresponding convolution.
options.explanation: A transposed convolution only restores the shape (it multiplies by the transposed weight matrix), not the original values. A convolution is generally not invertible, so the inverse is not recovered.

options.text: Overlapping filter contributions are summed in the output.
options.explanation: Each input entry scatters a scaled copy of the kernel into the output; where those copies overlap the contributions are added together.

options.text: Its output channel count must equal its input channel count.
options.explanation: The number of output channels is a free parameter (out_channels), exactly as in a normal convolution; a transposed convolution can map e.g. 12 channels to 6.

hints: Think of the transposed convolution as scattering the kernel over the output for each input entry.
Which hyperparameters are free in a transposed convolution?
explanation: A transposed convolution multiplies by the transpose of a convolution's weight matrix: every input value paints a scaled copy of the kernel onto the output, and overlapping copies are added. With stride greater than 1 it upsamples. It is not a true inverse (only the shape is reversed) and its channel counts are chosen freely.

title: Multihead attention projections and heads
prompt: Multihead self-attention has width $D=96$ and 6 equal-width heads. Count only $W_Q,W_K,W_V,W_O$, each a $96 \times 96$ matrix, with no biases. Which statements are correct?

options.text: With D fixed at 96, using 12 heads doubles these projection parameters.
options.explanation: The four matrices stay $96\times96$ whatever the number of heads, so the count remains $4D^2$. More heads only split the width into narrower slices (head dimension 8 for 12 heads).

options.text: Each head uses a separate full $96 \times 96$ matrix for each of Q, K and V.
options.explanation: Each head works on a $D/h=16$-dimensional slice of the single $96\times96$ projection, i.e. an effective $96\times16$ block per head. Full-size matrices per head would multiply the parameters by 6.

options.text: The four matrices contain 36,864 parameters in total.
options.explanation: Each matrix has $96\cdot96=9{,}216$ entries and there are four, so $4\cdot9{,}216=36{,}864$.

options.text: Each head has dimension 16.
options.explanation: Equal-width heads split the model width evenly: $96/6=16$.

hints: Compute $96^2$ and multiply by the number of matrices.
How is the model width divided among heads?
explanation: In standard multihead attention the Q, K, V and output projections are each $D\times D$, giving $4D^2=36{,}864$ weights for $D=96$ no matter how many heads there are. The heads are just a partition of the $D$ output columns into $h$ slices of size $D/h=16$. Changing the number of heads therefore changes the head dimension, not the parameter count.

title: Output height of a ConvTranspose2d
prompt: ConvTranspose2d maps 12 channels to 6 with kernel size 4, stride 2, padding 1, dilation 1 and output padding 0. For a $7 \times 7$ input, what is the output height?
hints: Use $H_{out}=(H_{in}-1)s-2p+d(k-1)+p_{out}+1$.
The channel numbers do not influence the spatial size.
explanation:
$$H_{out}=(7-1)\cdot2-2\cdot1+1\cdot(4-1)+0+1=12-2+3+1=14$$

Typical wrong results: 13 comes from dropping the final $+1$; 12 comes from using only $(H_{in}-1)s$ and ignoring the kernel and padding terms; 16 comes from forgetting to subtract $2p$ (12 + 3 + 1).

title: Pixel shuffle on an NCHW tensor
prompt: Pixel shuffle uses scale factor 2 on an NCHW tensor of shape $(2,20,9,11)$. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Its output shape is $(2,5,18,22)$.
options.explanation: Pixel shuffle maps $(N,C r^2,H,W)\to(N,C,rH,rW)$. With $r=2$: $20/4=5$ channels, $9\cdot2=18$ and $11\cdot2=22$.

options.text: It rearranges channels into spatial positions.
options.explanation: Each group of $r^2$ channels is interleaved into an $r\times r$ block of pixels (depth-to-space), trading channels for resolution.

options.text: It preserves the total number of tensor entries.
options.explanation: It is only a reshape/permutation: $2\cdot20\cdot9\cdot11=3960$ entries before and $2\cdot5\cdot18\cdot22=3960$ after.

options.text: The shuffle operation itself adds learned weights.
options.explanation: Pixel shuffle has no parameters; it just moves values around. Any learning happens in the convolution that produces the $Cr^2$ channels before it.

hints: Which channel count does the input need to have for scale factor $r$?
Does reshuffling values change how many there are?
explanation: Pixel shuffle (sub-pixel convolution) converts $Cr^2$ channels into $C$ channels at $r$ times the height and width. It is a parameter-free rearrangement, so the number of entries is unchanged, which is why it is a common alternative to transposed convolution for upsampling.

title: Output shape of a cross-attention layer
prompt:
An attention layer has 7 query rows of dimension 32 and 5 input rows of dimension 128. The key and value projection matrices $W_K$ and $W_V$ have shapes $(128,32)$ and $(128,48)$. It computes

$$Y=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\mathsf{T}}}{\sqrt{32}}\right)V.$$

Softmax is over keys. With no output projection, what is the output shape?

options.explanation: This is the shape of the transposed score matrix. The scores $QK^{\mathsf T}$ are $(7,5)$ and are multiplied by $V$, so this is not the final output.
The output width is the value dimension (48), not the query/key dimension (32). The dimension 32 only disappears in $QK^{\mathsf T}$.
This is the shape of $V$ itself. The output has one row per query (7), not per input row (5).
$Q$ is $(7,32)$, $K=XW_K$ is $(5,32)$ and $V=XW_V$ is $(5,48)$. Scores are $(7,5)$, and multiplying by $V$ gives $(7,5)\cdot(5,48)=(7,48)$.

hints: First find the shapes of $K$ and $V$ by projecting the 5 input rows.
The score matrix has one row per query and one column per key.
explanation: Keys and values come from the 5 input rows: $K=XW_K$ has shape $(5,32)$ and $V=XW_V$ has shape $(5,48)$. The scores $QK^{\mathsf T}$ have shape $(7,5)$ and the softmax over keys turns each row into weights summing to 1. Multiplying by $V$ gives $(7,48)$: one output row per query, whose width is the value dimension.

title: Parameters of a transformer block
prompt: A transformer block has width $D=64$ and MLP hidden width 256. Count the four $D\times D$ attention matrices, the two MLP matrices of shapes $(64,256)$ and $(256,64)$, and two LayerNorms, each with 64 scales and 64 shifts. Exclude attention and MLP biases. How many parameters are counted?
hints: Count the three groups separately: attention, MLP, LayerNorm.
Each LayerNorm has a scale and a shift for every one of the 64 features.
explanation:
Attention: $4\cdot64\cdot64=16{,}384$. MLP: $64\cdot256+256\cdot64=32{,}768$. LayerNorms: $2\cdot(64+64)=256$. Total: $16{,}384+32{,}768+256=49{,}408$.

Typical wrong results: 49,152 leaves out the LayerNorms; 49,280 counts only one LayerNorm (128); 65,792 is 16,384 larger than the correct total, as if there were four extra $64\times64$ matrices.

title: Self-attention under token permutation
prompt: With fixed weights, an unmasked self-attention layer has no positional encoding, position-dependent bias or dropout. The input tokens are permuted. What happens to the output?

options.text: The output token vectors are permuted in the same way.
options.explanation: Output $i$ is $\sum_j \text{softmax}_j(q_i\cdot k_j/\sqrt d)\,v_j$, a sum over all tokens that does not depend on their order. Permuting the inputs permutes $q,k,v$ identically, so each output vector keeps its value and just moves with its token (permutation equivariance).

options.text: Every output vector necessarily becomes zero.
options.explanation: Nothing in the attention computation forces zeros: the weights, softmax and values are all still defined and give the same vectors as before, only reordered.

options.text: The output sequence must stay in exactly its old order.
options.explanation: The output rows are tied to their input tokens, so they move along with the permutation; attention has no mechanism that restores the original order.

options.text: The layer must be retrained before accepting the permutation.
options.explanation: The weights are shared across positions and do not encode any particular order, so the same weights remain valid for any permutation and no retraining is needed.

hints: Write output $i$ as a sum over all tokens $j$.
Does a sum over $j$ care about the order of its terms?
explanation: Without positional information, self-attention treats its input as a set: every token's query, key and value depend only on that token, and each output is a weighted sum over all tokens. Permuting the inputs therefore permutes the outputs in the same way. This is why transformers add positional encodings (or masks / relative biases) whenever order matters.

title: ViT patches and dense reconstruction
prompt: A ViT splits a $128 \times 128$ image into nonoverlapping $16 \times 16$ patches, with no class token. A shared linear head maps each token to a 4-channel $16 \times 16$ output patch. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The reconstructed dense output has shape $4 \times 128 \times 128$.
options.explanation: The $8\times8$ grid of patches, each $16\times16$, tiles the full $128\times128$ area, and every patch has 4 channels, giving $4\times128\times128$.

options.text: There are 128 patch tokens.
options.explanation: 128 is only the image side length. There are $128/16=8$ patches along each side, so $8\cdot8=64$ tokens.

options.text: The linear head outputs 1,024 values per token.
options.explanation: Each token is mapped to a 4-channel $16\times16$ patch, i.e. $4\cdot16\cdot16=1{,}024$ values.

options.text: There are 64 patch tokens.
options.explanation: The patch grid is $(128/16)\times(128/16)=8\times8=64$ tokens, and no class token is added.

hints: Divide the image side by the patch side to get the grid size.
How many values does a 4-channel 16×16 patch contain?
explanation: Non-overlapping patches give an $8\times8$ grid, i.e. 64 tokens. A shared linear head turns each token into $4\cdot16\cdot16=1{,}024$ numbers, which are reshaped to a 4-channel $16\times16$ patch; tiling the 64 patches back together gives a dense $4\times128\times128$ output. This is the standard way of getting per-pixel predictions from a plain ViT.

title: BatchNorm with tiny batches and the GroupNorm alternative
prompt: A network is trained with only 2 images per device and uses BatchNorm. Explain what goes wrong with BatchNorm's statistics during training, why evaluation mode uses running averages instead of batch statistics, and why GroupNorm is a better fit for this setting.
model_answer: In training mode BatchNorm normalizes each channel with the mean and variance of the current mini-batch. With only 2 images these estimates are very noisy, and every sample's output depends on its batch neighbours, which adds noise and creates a mismatch with test time. In evaluation mode the output should be deterministic and independent of other test samples (even for a batch of one), so BatchNorm uses running averages of the mean and variance collected during training. GroupNorm computes the statistics per sample over groups of channels and spatial positions, so it does not depend on the batch size, behaves identically in training and evaluation and needs no running statistics.
key_points: BatchNorm's batch mean and variance are noisy estimates when the batch is tiny.
Each output depends on the other samples in the batch, causing a train/test mismatch.
Evaluation uses running mean and variance accumulated during training so predictions are deterministic.
GroupNorm normalizes within each sample over channel groups, independent of batch size and with no running statistics.
hints: Which axes does BatchNorm average over?
What would a single test image's batch statistics look like?
explanation: The key idea is where the statistics come from: BatchNorm averages across the batch dimension, so its quality depends on the batch size and it needs stored running estimates for inference. GroupNorm averages within a sample, which removes both the batch-size dependence and the train/eval difference. Common half-answers only say that 'GroupNorm works better' without naming the batch-dimension dependence, or claim that GroupNorm enlarges the batch, which it does not.

title: Why self-attention needs positional information
prompt: Explain why a self-attention layer without any positional information is permutation equivariant, what this means for tasks such as language modelling or ViT patch processing, and how the problem is fixed.
model_answer: In self-attention each token's query, key and value depend only on that token, and output $i$ is a softmax-weighted sum of the values of all tokens. A sum over tokens does not depend on their order, so permuting the input rows permutes the queries, keys and values the same way and each output vector keeps its value and simply moves to the new position. The layer therefore cannot tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog' or know where a patch lies in an image. Adding positional encodings (or position-dependent biases) to the inputs, or using causal masks, breaks this symmetry and injects order information.
key_points: Q, K and V of a token depend only on that token, and the output is a sum over all tokens, which ignores order.
Permuting the inputs permutes the outputs in the same way (equivariance), with the same values.
Without extra information the model cannot use word order or patch location.
Positional encodings, position-dependent biases or masks supply the missing order information.
hints: Write output $i$ as a sum over all tokens $j$.
What would the model see if two sentences contained the same words in a different order?
explanation: Attention compares tokens by content only, so order is invisible unless it is added to the input. The correct answer links the order-independent sum to the equivariance property and then names a remedy (positional encodings, relative biases or causal masking). A common mistake is to say the output is unchanged (invariant) instead of permuted, or to think that retraining alone can fix it: without positional information no weights can distinguish the orderings.

title: Min-max scaling of an out-of-range test value
prompt: A min-max scaler is fitted on a training set whose values range from 4 to 12 and maps this range to $[0, 1]$. There is no clipping and no epsilon. What does the scaler output for a test value of 16? Give the answer with 2 decimals.
hints: The scaler uses the training minimum and maximum, even for test values.
Write the formula $(x - x_{\min}) / (x_{\max} - x_{\min})$ and plug in the numbers.
explanation:
Min-max scaling computes $$x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$$ with the minimum and maximum taken from the training data: $x' = \frac{16 - 4}{12 - 4} = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$.

A test value outside the training range is mapped outside $[0, 1]$ because nothing clips it. Typical wrong results: 1 would be the output for the training maximum 12 (or for a clipped value), 0.5 comes from $\frac{16 - 12}{8}$, which measures the distance to the maximum instead of to the minimum, and 2 comes from dividing by 8 without subtracting the minimum ($16 / 8$).

title: PCA rotation versus PCA whitening
prompt: Full-dimensional PCA is fitted to centered training data whose covariance matrix is positive definite. In exact arithmetic, which statements hold for the transformed training data?

options.text: PCA whitening additionally rescales each principal component to unit variance.
options.explanation: After the rotation the component variances are the covariance eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Whitening divides component $i$ by $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$, which makes every variance equal to 1 (possible because the covariance is positive definite, so all $\lambda_i > 0$).

options.text: PCA whitening requires the original features to be statistically independent.
options.explanation: Whitening needs no independence assumption: it only uses the covariance matrix, and it produces uncorrelated components with unit variance. Uncorrelated is weaker than independent, and whitening does not remove higher-order dependence.

options.text: PCA rotation alone guarantees unit variance for every component.
options.explanation: A rotation preserves total variance and gives each component the variance of its eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, which can be any positive number. Unit variance only appears after the extra rescaling step of whitening.

options.text: PCA rotation diagonalizes the feature covariance.
options.explanation: Projecting onto the eigenvectors $V$ of the covariance gives a new covariance $V^\top \Sigma V = \Lambda$, which is diagonal, so the rotated components are uncorrelated.

hints: Write the covariance of the rotated data in terms of the eigendecomposition $\Sigma = V \Lambda V^\top$.
What do the diagonal entries of $\Lambda$ equal, and what would you divide by to make them 1?
explanation: PCA is two separable ideas. The rotation onto the eigenvectors of the covariance decorrelates the features: the new covariance is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues, so the components are uncorrelated but have different variances. Whitening adds a rescaling by the inverse square roots of the eigenvalues so that every component has variance 1 and the covariance becomes the identity. Neither step needs the features to be independent, only the second moments are used.

title: Standardizing a feature value
prompt: A feature has training mean 12 and training standard deviation 4. Ignoring epsilon, what is the standardized value (z-score) of the value 18? Give the answer with 2 decimals.
hints: Standardization first centers the value, then scales it.
Use the training statistics, not statistics computed from the new value.
explanation:
Standardization computes $$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{18 - 12}{4} = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5$$ so 18 lies one and a half standard deviations above the training mean.

Typical wrong results: 6 is only the centered value $18 - 12$ (the division by $\sigma$ was forgotten), 4.5 comes from dividing 18 by 4 without subtracting the mean, and 0.5 comes from dividing the centered value by the mean 12 instead of the standard deviation 4.

title: Two hidden units with identical parameters
prompt: Two hidden units in the same dense layer have the same activation function, identical incoming weights and biases, and identical outgoing weights. Training uses gradient descent with no neuron-specific randomness. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Their different neuron indices automatically force different learned features.
options.explanation: The index of a neuron is only a label and does not enter any computation. Two units that start with identical parameters receive identical gradients, so they stay identical; something random or asymmetric must break the tie.

options.text: They initially compute the same function.
options.explanation: Both units apply the same activation to the same weighted sum of the same inputs (same incoming weights and bias), so their outputs are equal for every input.

options.text: Their parameters remain identical after gradient-descent updates.
options.explanation: Equal outputs and equal outgoing weights mean each unit has the same influence on the loss, so the gradients of their incoming weights, biases and outgoing weights are equal. Applying the same update to the same values keeps them equal at every step.

options.text: Replacing all zero weights with the same nonzero constant necessarily breaks their symmetry.
options.explanation: A constant initialization is still the same for every unit, so the units remain exact copies. Breaking symmetry requires different values per unit, which is why weights are initialized randomly.

hints: Compare the gradient that each of the two units receives.
What would a constant, nonzero initialization change about the difference between the two units?
explanation: If two hidden units have identical incoming and outgoing parameters, they compute the same output and contribute identically to the loss, so their gradients are identical. Gradient descent applies identical updates and the units stay identical forever, wasting capacity. This is why weights are initialized randomly: random values break the symmetry. Constant initialization, zero or nonzero, does not.

title: Parameters of a small two-layer MLP
prompt: An MLP has layer widths 5 -> 3 -> 2: a dense layer from 5 to 3 units, a ReLU, and a dense layer from 3 to 2 units. Each dense layer has one bias per output neuron. ReLU has no parameters. How many trainable parameters does the model have?
hints: A dense layer from $n$ inputs to $m$ outputs has $n \cdot m$ weights and $m$ biases.
Count each dense layer separately and add them.
explanation:
First dense layer: $5 \cdot 3 = 15$ weights plus 3 biases = 18. Second dense layer: $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ weights plus 2 biases = 8. ReLU adds nothing. Total: $18 + 8 = 26$.

Common wrong results: 21 counts only the weights ($15 + 6$) and forgets all biases; 23 gives biases only to the second layer ($15 + 6 + 2$); 31 adds 5 extra biases for the input features, although biases belong to output neurons only, so the inputs have none.

title: Robust scaling with median and IQR
prompt: A feature has training median 30, first quartile 20 and third quartile 40. Robust scaling subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range (IQR). Ignoring epsilon, what is the scaled value of 60? Give the answer with 2 decimals.
hints: The IQR is the difference between the third and the first quartile.
Subtract the median first, then divide by the IQR.
explanation:
The interquartile range is $\text{IQR} = 40 - 20 = 20$. The scaled value is $$\frac{x - \text{median}}{\text{IQR}} = \frac{60 - 30}{20} = \frac{30}{20} = 1.5$$

Typical wrong results: 1 divides by the median 30 instead of the IQR; 2 subtracts the first quartile instead of the median, $\frac{60 - 20}{20}$; 30 is only the centered value and is missing the division by the IQR.

title: Splitting data with several scans per patient
prompt: A dataset has several scans per patient. To evaluate performance on unseen patients, which split is most appropriate?

options.text: Put exact duplicate scans into different splits to balance sizes.
options.explanation: If the same scan is in the training and the test set, the model is evaluated on data it has already seen, which inflates the measured performance. Splits must be disjoint, and balancing sizes is never a reason to duplicate.

options.text: Choose the test scans after comparing models on their test accuracy.
options.explanation: Selecting the test set (or the model) based on test accuracy uses the test data for decisions, so the test result becomes an optimistic, biased estimate. Model selection belongs on a separate validation set, and the test set should be fixed beforehand.

options.text: Randomly split scans so every patient appears in every split.
options.explanation: Scans of the same patient are highly correlated, so a random scan-level split lets the model see the patient during training and be tested on the same patient. That measures performance on known patients, not on unseen ones.

options.text: Keep all scans from a patient in one split.
options.explanation: A group-wise split by patient guarantees that no patient in the test set was seen during training, so the test score estimates how the model performs on new patients.

hints: What is the unit that must be 'unseen' at test time: a scan or a patient?
Which splitting mistakes let information from the test set reach training?
explanation: The test set should mimic the deployment situation. If the model will be applied to new patients, the split must be done at the patient level (group-wise), so that all scans of a patient lie in exactly one of training, validation or test. Splitting at the scan level leaks patient-specific information into training, and tuning on the test set or duplicating samples across splits also gives overly optimistic results.

title: Accuracy and recall on an imbalanced dataset
prompt: A classifier predicts negative for all 950 negative and all 50 positive examples. Positive-class recall is the fraction of actual positives that are predicted positive. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Its accuracy is 95%.
options.explanation: All 950 negatives are classified correctly and all 50 positives are wrong, so accuracy is $950 / 1000 = 95\%$.

options.text: Its positive-class recall is 95%.
options.explanation: Recall only looks at actual positives: 0 of the 50 are found, so it is $0 / 50 = 0\%$. The 95% is the accuracy, which is dominated by the negatives.

options.text: Its accuracy alone proves that it detects the rare class well.
options.explanation: A trivial classifier that always predicts the majority class reaches 95% accuracy without detecting a single positive. With imbalanced classes, accuracy hides failures on the rare class.

options.text: Its positive-class recall is 0%.
options.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by actual positives: $0 / 50 = 0\%$, since no positive is predicted positive.

hints: Count true positives, true negatives and the number of actual positives.
Compare what accuracy counts with what recall counts.
explanation: Accuracy averages over all examples, so with 95% negatives a model that always says negative scores 95%. Recall focuses on the positive class: true positives divided by actual positives, here $0 / 50 = 0\%$. On imbalanced data, report class-specific metrics such as recall and precision in addition to accuracy, because accuracy can look excellent for a useless model.

title: Mean and variance after a scale and shift
prompt: Let $Z$ have mean 0 and variance 1. Define $W = 0.04 Z - 0.2$. Compute the mean and the variance of $W$. Give the mean with 3 decimals and the variance with 4 decimals.
hints: A constant shift changes the mean but not the variance.
Multiplying by a constant $a$ multiplies the variance by $a^2$.
explanation:
For $W = aZ + b$ we have $\mathbb{E}[W] = a\,\mathbb{E}[Z] + b$ and $\text{Var}(W) = a^2\,\text{Var}(Z)$. With $a = 0.04$ and $b = -0.2$: the mean is $0.04 \cdot 0 - 0.2 = -0.2$ and the variance is $0.04^2 \cdot 1 = 0.0016$.

Typical wrong results: a variance of 0.04 forgets to square the factor (0.04 is the standard deviation, not the variance); a mean of 0.04 and variance of 0.2 mix up the scale and the shift; mean 0 and variance 1 ignore the transformation completely.

title: Prediction in original units after target standardization
prompt: A regression target is standardized as $y_{\text{norm}} = \frac{y - 80}{16}$. The model predicts $y_{\text{norm}} = 1.25$. What is the prediction in the original units of $y$?
hints: Invert the standardization: solve the formula for $y$.
Multiply by the scale first, then add the shift.
explanation:
Solving $y_{\text{norm}} = \frac{y - 80}{16}$ for $y$ gives $y = 16\,y_{\text{norm}} + 80 = 16 \cdot 1.25 + 80 = 20 + 80 = 100$.

Typical wrong results: 81.25 adds the prediction to the mean without rescaling ($80 + 1.25$); 0.078125 divides instead of multiplying ($1.25 / 16$); 20 multiplies by 16 but forgets to add the mean 80 back.

title: Where should scaling statistics come from?
prompt: A min-max scaler, a standardizer and a robust scaler all need statistics (minimum and maximum, mean and standard deviation, or median and quartiles). Explain why these statistics must be computed on the training set only and then reused unchanged for validation and test data, and what happens to a test value that lies outside the training range.
model_answer: The scaler is part of the model, so its parameters must be estimated from training data only. Computing them on the test data would leak information about the test distribution into preprocessing and make the evaluation optimistic, and the same input would be transformed differently at training and at deployment time. Reusing the training statistics means a test value outside the training range is simply mapped outside the nominal range, for example 16 becomes 1.5 under min-max scaling with range [4, 12], unless clipping is added. That is expected and informative, not an error.
key_points: The scaling parameters are fitted on the training set only, like any other learned parameter.
Fitting them on validation or test data leaks information and gives an optimistic evaluation.
The same transformation must be applied to all splits and at deployment so that inputs mean the same thing.
Out-of-range test values are mapped outside the nominal range (e.g. above 1 for min-max) unless clipping is used.
hints: Treat the scaler as a part of the model that has to be trained.
What would the transformation of a single new sample depend on in deployment?
explanation: The key idea is that preprocessing statistics are learned parameters and obey the same rule as the weights: estimate them on training data, then freeze them. A frequent half-answer is only 'to avoid leakage', without noting that deployment requires a fixed transformation for single samples. Another mistake is to think out-of-range values must be clipped or are errors; with the frozen training statistics they are just mapped outside the usual range (1.5 for the value 16 with training range 4 to 12).

title: Why identical neurons never differentiate
prompt: Explain why two hidden units of the same layer that start with identical incoming weights, biases and outgoing weights remain identical throughout gradient-descent training, and why initializing all weights to the same nonzero constant does not solve this. How does random initialization fix it?
model_answer: Two units with identical parameters compute the same output for every input and affect the loss in exactly the same way, so the gradients with respect to their parameters are identical. Gradient descent then applies the same update to both, and they remain copies forever, so the layer behaves as if it had fewer units. A constant nonzero initialization still gives every unit the same parameters, so the symmetry persists. Random initialization gives each unit different weights, so they compute different functions, receive different gradients and can learn different features.
key_points: Identical parameters give identical outputs and therefore identical gradients for the two units.
Identical updates keep the parameters identical at every step, so the units stay copies.
A constant nonzero initialization is still identical across units, so it does not break the symmetry.
Random initialization makes the units differ at the start, which leads to different gradients and different features.
hints: Think about what the gradient of each unit depends on.
Is the difference between zero and a nonzero constant relevant for symmetry?
explanation: The argument is an induction: if the two units are equal now, their gradients are equal, so they are still equal after the update. The common mistake is to believe that nonzero values or different neuron indices are enough; what matters is that the units differ from each other, not that the weights are nonzero. A half-answer that only says 'random initialization avoids zero weights' misses the symmetry argument.
